food.text: Byzantine trading with foreigners brought in grains, sugar, livestock, fruits, vegetables and spices that would otherwise have been limited to specific climates. Byzantine cuisine continued local ancient Greek, ancient Roman and Mediterranean cooking, and trade widened it.
Byzantine citizens slaughtered pigs at the beginning of winter. This gave their families sausages, salt pork and lard for the whole year.

Bread played a major part in the Byzantine diet, and the most valued loaf was made from finely sieved wheat flour with no other grains mixed in. Barley was valued less than wheat and sold for a lower price.

Cooks experimented with many new combinations of food and created two styles. One was eastern, found in Asia Minor and the eastern Aegean, and mixed Byzantine cooking with trade items. The other was a leaner style based on local Greek food culture.
Byzantine citizens hunted deer and wild boar, a favourite and distinguished occupation of men. They usually hunted with dogs and hawks, though sometimes they used trapping, netting and bird-liming.
Only upper middle and higher Byzantines could afford lamb. Beef was seldom eaten, because cattle were needed to cultivate the fields.
Beehives kept by Byzantine Greeks let citizens gather and sell honey on a large scale, and honey appeared in cooking, pastry and tea recipes. In 1152 a tax was introduced on beekeeping.
Millet was not prized by Byzantine authors, and Anna Komnene called it "food of barbarians". Rye, millet, oats and vetch were mostly grown as animal fodder rather than for people to eat.
Millet was used to make gruel and porridge such as trachanas. Symeon Seth also mentions poor people eating millet mixed with milk.

A 14th-century Last Supper fresco at the Dochiariou monastery on Mount Athos shows food in several bowls, with wine jugs, beakers, individual bread rolls, and shared dishes and knives. It offers a glimpse of how Byzantine tables may have looked.

When Mehmed II took Constantinople in 1453, the Turks gained control of the spice trade in the eastern Mediterranean. Health tonics made by the palace confectionery could include up to 60 different spices.
Archaeology supports the idea that knives were used as eating utensils in the 14th century. Evidence comes from excavations of medieval Panakton.

art.text: Byzantine art grew from the art of ancient Greece and never lost sight of its classical heritage before 1453. But the humanist ethic of ancient Greek art was replaced by the Christian ethic. If classical art glorified man, Byzantine art aimed to glorify God.

Monumental sculpture with figures remained a taboo in Byzantine art, and hardly any exceptions are known. Small ivory reliefs were a speciality instead, almost all in the iconic mode. Relief decoration on bowls and other metal objects was also a speciality.

The Cretan School of icon painting flourished while Crete was under Venetian rule during the late Middle Ages. Its artists developed a particular style under the influence of both Eastern and Western artistic traditions. It became the central force in Greek painting during the 15th, 16th and 17th centuries.

The Palace of the Grand Master of the Knights of Rhodes is one of the few examples of Gothic architecture in Greece. The Knights Hospitaller occupied Rhodes in 1309 and converted a Byzantine fortress into their administrative centre and the Grand Master's palace.
art.source_title: Palace of the Grand Master of the Knights of Rhodes

art.text: Byzantine art abandoned the classical attempt to imitate reality as closely as possible. Its most salient feature was an abstract, anti-naturalistic character, with a more symbolic approach. Byzantine painting concentrated mainly on icons and hagiographies.

Churches built after the end of Iconoclasm, such as the monastery church of Hosios Lukas in Greece (c. 1000) and the Daphni Monastery near Athens (c. 1050), followed the cross-in-square plan. Their design and decoration became more standardized after Iconoclasm ended.

The richest Byzantine interiors were finished with thin plates of marble or coloured and patterned stone. Wall mosaics with a gold background became standard for the grandest buildings, while frescos were a cheaper alternative.

The Medieval City of Rhodes was constructed around 1309 to 1523. The high town in the north was entirely built by the Hospitallers, and the whole medieval city sits within a wall 4 km long. It was added to the UNESCO World Heritage list in 1988.

Basil I's votive church of the Theotokos of the Pharos and the Nea Ekklesia, both no longer existent, are presumed to have served as models for most cross-in-square sanctuaries of the Macedonian dynasty. These include Nea Moni of Chios, described as a pet project of Constantine IX.

In Middle Byzantine architecture, cloisonné masonry refers to walls built with a regular mix of stone and brick, often with more brick. The exterior of the 11th- or 12th-century Pammakaristos Church in Istanbul is an example of this technique.

Byzantine architecture persisted in Bulgaria, Greece, Serbia, Romania, North Macedonia and other Orthodox countries even after the empire fell. From the 16th up to the 18th centuries it gave birth to local post-Byzantine schools of architecture.

Around 1310, a highly ornate parekklesion was added to the Pammakaristos Church in Constantinople for the tomb of Michael Glabas Tarchaniotes. It shows the attenuated proportions favored in the late Byzantine era, along with shifts in how the mosaics treated figures.

war.text: In 1354 the Ottomans crossed into Europe and seized Gallipoli. From there they advanced through Thrace, taking Demotika, Philippopolis and finally Adrianople by 1369. By 1370 most of Thrace was under Ottoman control, bringing them into direct contact with the Serbian lords.

The Albanian leader Skanderbeg fended off Ottoman attacks for more than 25 years. His victories included the Battle of Torvioll and the siege of Krujë, culminating in a decisive win at the Battle of Albulena in 1457. He died on 17 January 1468, after which Lekë Dukagjini led the resistance until 1479.

On 15 March 1311 the Catalan Company defeated the Frankish Duchy of Athens at the Battle of Halmyros. Duke Walter of Brienne had hired the mercenaries, then refused to pay them and prepared to expel them by force. The Catalans were considerably outnumbered, yet they chose the battleground and stood behind marshy terrain, which they further inundated. Walter and almost the entire knighthood of his realm fell in the field.

On 26 September 1371 an Ottoman force under Lala Şahin Pasha and Hacı İlbey met a Serbian coalition near the Maritsa River. Ottoman ghazi warriors attacked the Serbian camp at night while most of the soldiers were asleep, and the army was massacred along with its commanders. Both Serbian commanders, King Vukašin Mrnjavčević and Despot Jovan Uglješa, were killed. Konstantin Jireček wrote that the men were slaughtered "in such numbers that the river ran red with their blood."

The Ottoman–Venetian wars began in 1423 and lasted until 1718. They included the fall of Negroponte in 1470. The Venetian-ruled island of Corfu remained the only Greek island never conquered by the Ottomans.

Around 1358 or 1359, Albanian tribesmen under Karl Thopia destroyed the army of Nikephoros II Orsini, ruler of the Despotate of Epirus, near the river Achelous in Aetolia. The Albanians inflicted heavy casualties on his forces, and Orsini himself was killed during the fighting. Epirus was then divided among Albanian clans, and only Ioannina remained under Greek governance.

At Maritsa the Serbian army was massacred and annihilated, and according to historian Ion Grumeza the Serbian Empire lost a large proportion of its ruling aristocracy in the battle. After the Ottoman victory, several regional lords, including Vukašin's son Prince Marko, became Ottoman vassals, obliged to provide tribute and military service. Emperor Uroš V died childless later that year, ending the Nemanjić line.
In 1465 Ballaban's Campaign was launched against Skanderbeg with the goal of crushing the Albanian resistance. It was not successful and ended in an Albanian victory.

At Halmyros, Walter of Brienne, confident in his heavy cavalry, charged headlong at the Catalan line. In Gregoras' account, the Frankish knights got stuck in the mud and the Almogavars, lightly armed with swords and darts, dispatched them in their heavy armour. The Catalans defeated the charge, and the Duke and most of his men fell. The Catalans then cut off Walter's head. The battle is seen as part of a shift in European warfare that began with the Battle of the Golden Spurs in 1302, when infantry successfully challenged knightly heavy cavalry.

In 1344 a Serbian army under Preljub attacked a 3,100-strong Aydin force returning to Anatolia to defend Smyrna. It was said to be the first battle between the Serbs and Turks. The Turks won, but could not stop Stefan Dušan's conquest of Byzantine Macedonia.

Estimates of the armies at Maritsa are unreliable. The Serbian Monk Isaiah claimed 60,000 Serbs, and later Ottoman chroniclers offered 60,000 Serbs against 4,000 Ottomans. Aleksandar Shopov argues that the forces most probably did not exceed ten thousand soldiers, since even armies of a few thousand were considered large.

After Halmyros, almost the entire Frankish elite of Athens lay dead on the field or in captivity. The Catalans asked their captive Boniface of Verona to lead them, but he declined, so they chose Roger Deslaur. Many of the Catalans took the widows and mothers of the very men they had slain at Halmyros as their wives. They then turned to Frederick II of Sicily, whose son Manfred became Duke of Athens. Alfonso Fadrique expanded the Duchy into Thessaly, establishing the Duchy of Neopatras in 1319.

literature.text: The Digenes Akritas, a collection of heroic sagas from the 12th century, was the first literary work written completely in the vernacular. It was later collated in a verse epic in fifteen-syllable verse. It dealt with ancient and medieval heroic sagas, and also with stories of animals and plants.

Byzantine literature was marked by diglossy, meaning two distinct forms of Greek were in use. One was a scholarly dialect based on Attic Greek, and the other was a vernacular based on Koine Greek. Writers could choose between them depending on their audience.

Digenes Akritas is the most famous of the Acritic songs and is often regarded as the only surviving epic poem from the Byzantine Empire. Some consider it to signal the beginnings of modern Greek literature.

The Chronicle of the Morea is a verse chronicle from the 14th century that is described as unique. It survives in French, Italian and Aragonese versions as well as Greek. It covers the history of Frankish feudalism on the Peloponnese during the Latinokratia of the Principality of Achaea.

Anna Komnena wrote the Alexiad, a biography of her father, Emperor Alexios I Komnenos, about a century after Psellos's Chronography of the mid 11th century. Both works belonged to an Attic renaissance under the dynasty of the Komnenoi. The vernacular verse epic appeared in the 12th century almost as a backlash against it.

Digenes Akritas began as a collection of heroic sagas from the 12th century, later collated into a verse epic. It was the first literary work written entirely in the vernacular. It appeared almost as a backlash to the Attic renaissance under the Komnenoi.

The Alexiad is the biography of Emperor Alexios I Komnenos, written by his daughter Anna Komnena about a century after Psellos's Chronography of the mid-11th century. Both works belong to the Attic renaissance under the Komnenoi dynasty.

The Chronicle of the Morea is a unique 14th-century verse chronicle. It covers the history of Frankish feudalism on the Peloponnese during the Latinokratia of the Principality of Achaea, a crusader state set up after the Fourth Crusade. It has also been preserved in French, Italian and Aragonese versions.

Medieval Greek fables about animals were popular. The Tale about Quadrupeds, dated to 1364, describes a meeting of all the animals at the invitation of their king, the lion. The Poulologos is a similar tale about birds.
The Digenes Akritas is composed in fifteen-syllable verse, known as versus politicus. It deals with ancient and medieval heroic sagas, but also with stories of animals and plants.

The Synaxarion of the Estimable Donkey is a 14th-century fable of a donkey travelling to the Holy Land with a wolf and a fox. The Porikologos, about fruits, was written in prose as a parody of the official language of the Byzantine court.
Spaneas, a poem containing moral advice for a young man, was frequently copied. Story of Ptocholeon is one of the earliest allegorical and didactic poems and has oriental origins, probably Indian.

John VI Cantacuzene, a 14th-century historian, narrated his own achievements in a self-complacent manner. Nicephorus Gregoras, also of the 14th century, was a man of the world well versed in philosophy and the classics. Though subjective on internal Byzantine affairs, these writers are trustworthy on external events.

Emmanuel Georgillas, also called Limenitis, wrote The Plague of Rhodes, a narrative poem about the plague that hit the city of Rhodes in 1498. Rhodes was then held by the Knights Hospitaller, and although lyric poetry was popular there, only a few texts survive.

science.text: The counterweight trebuchet was invented in the Byzantine Empire during the reign of Alexios I Komnenos (1081–1118). The Byzantines used the new siege weapon to devastate citadels and fortifications. Armies of Europe and Asia eventually learned and adopted it.

Byzantine scientist Symeon Seth offered proofs that the earth is a sphere. He noted that when it is afternoon in Persia, it is still morning in Byzantine lands. He also pointed out that some stars seen in the north are not seen in the south.

Medicine was a science in which the Byzantines improved on their Greco-Roman predecessors, starting from Galen. The hospital appeared in the Byzantine Empire as an institution offering medical care and the possibility of a cure, because of the ideals of Christian charity. Byzantine medicine influenced both Islamic and Renaissance medicine.

Gregory Chioniades, born in Constantinople around 1240, traveled to Persia to learn astronomy. He brought back astronomical texts that he translated into Greek, and founded an astronomical academy at Trebizond. He also served as Orthodox bishop in Tabriz.

Gregory Chioniades translated the astronomical tables of his teacher Shams al-Din al-Bukhari, who had worked at the Maragheh observatory under Nasir al-Din al-Tusi. He also translated the Persian Zij-i Ilkhani by al-Tusi and the Maragheh observatory into Greek.
Nicephorus Gregoras is known to have predicted with exactitude a total solar eclipse on 16 July 1330. He used Ptolemy's Handy Tables and Almagest. In astronomy, he was a pupil of Theodore Metochites.

Theodore Metochites began learning astronomy from Manuel Bryennios in 1312/13. He later wrote an introduction to the study of Ptolemaic astronomy, the Stoicheiosis astronomike. He also became the teacher of Nicephorus Gregoras.

Chioniades helped transmit innovations from the Islamic world to Europe. These include the universal latitude-independent astrolabe and a Greek description of the Tusi couple, which would later have an influence on Copernican heliocentrism.

In 1326 Nicephorus Gregoras proposed reforms to the calendar in a treatise that still exists. Emperor Andronicus II refused to carry them out for fear of disturbances. Over two hundred years later, Gregory XIII introduced them on almost the same lines.

Manuel Bryennios taught astronomy, mathematics and music theory in Constantinople around 1300. His only surviving work is the Harmonika, a three-volume codification of Byzantine musical scholarship. It draws on Ptolemy, Nicomachus and the Neopythagorean authors.

The physician Nicholas Myrepsos was at the court of John III Doukas Vatatzes at Nicaea when a solar eclipse took place on October 6, 1241, shortly before the death of the empress Irene. The emperor held him in great esteem, and he attained the dignity of actuarius. His compendium on medical science is still extant, though it is chiefly compiled from former writers and contains many superstitious remedies.

politics.text: In 1346, Stefan Dušan was crowned Emperor of the Serbs and Greeks in Skoplje by the Serbian Patriarch, on April 16. The Byzantines received this with indignation. His goal was to become the successor of the Byzantine Emperors.

The Fourth Crusade was originally intended to target Egypt. Instead, the crusaders attacked Constantinople in 1203 and reinstated Isaac II and his son Alexios Angelos on the throne. The new rulers swiftly grew unpopular and were deposed by Alexios V. The crusaders used this as a pretext to sack the city in April 1204, ransacking the accumulated wealth of Constantinople. The sack destroyed centuries of its wealth and fragmented the empire.

After the Sack of Constantinople in 1204, French and Italian states, fiefs and colonies were carved out of the partitioned Byzantine Empire. Orthodox Greeks called the Western newcomers Franks, giving the period its name, Frankokratia. Some areas stayed under Frankish control, especially Venetian, until the Ottoman conquest.

The Serbian Empire, established in 1346 by Dušan the Mighty, was the most powerful state in Southeast Europe. It stretched from the Danube in the north to the Gulf of Corinth in the south, with its capital in Skopje. Dušan also promoted the Serbian Archbishopric to a Patriarchate.

Stefan Dečanski was overthrown in 1331 by his son, Stefan Dušan. Taking advantage of the Byzantine civil war of 1341 to 1347, Dušan doubled his kingdom's size at Byzantium's expense. He conquered almost all of present-day Greece except the Peloponnese and the islands.

The Serbian Empire effectively ended with the death of Uroš V in 1371, who died childless on 4 December 1371. That year the Ottomans defeated the Serbs under Vukašin at the Battle of Maritsa, where much of the Serbian nobility was killed by the Ottoman Turks, and the southern governors became Ottoman vassals. With no heir agreed upon, semi-independent provincial lords, who often feuded with each other, ruled the empire.

The Asen dynasty rose to lead Bulgaria after a rebellion against the Byzantine Empire at the turn of 1185/1186, caused by an increase in imperial taxes. It founded the Second Bulgarian Empire, which the dynasty ruled until 1280.

When civil war returned to Byzantium in 1341, John VI Kantakouzenos appealed to Dušan and was granted asylum in Serbia. Dušan later ceased his support and switched sides. Kantakouzenos then turned to Turks for help, and Turks entered European soil for the first time.

Lazar Hrebeljanović, a duke in central Serbia, stood against the Ottomans at the Battle of Kosovo in 1389. The result was indecisive but led to the subsequent fall of Serbia. His son Stefan Lazarević was an Ottoman vassal by 1394, then became a Hungarian ally in 1402.

The Principality of Achaea, covering the Peloponnese, quickly became the strongest Frankish state after 1205. Its main rival, the Byzantine Despotate of the Morea, eventually conquered it. In the 1380s it fell under the Navarrese Company, which ended vassalage to the Angevin kings of Naples in 1404.

In 1204 Pope Innocent III addressed Kaloyan as King of Bulgarians and Vlachs. In reply, Kaloyan called himself Emperor of all Bulgarians and Vlachs, though he signed himself Emperor Kaloyan of Bulgaria.

When a Bulgarian monarch died without a legitimate heir, the nobility customarily elected an emperor from among themselves. Constantine Tikh, George I Terter and Michael Shishman were all chosen this way.

philosophy.text: In 1054 the dynamic papacy of Pope Leo IX precipitated the East-West Schism. It split the Latin Church from the Eastern Orthodox Church of the Byzantine Empire after centuries of growing rivalry.

Plethon formed a circle of students at Mystras, in the Despotate of the Morea. Many ethnic Greeks today trace their teachings and practices through Plethon and his students, and credit them with the survival of the tradition.

The Balkans had converted to Christianity by the 11th century, but it was influenced by Orthodox Christianity and Bogomilism. This kept the region a religious border zone to Catholic Europe. In an age when religion decided who could legitimately be enslaved, that status fed the Balkan slave trade.

In 1219 the Serbian Orthodox Church was reorganized as an autocephalous archbishopric headed by Saint Sava. This happened shortly after Stefan the First-Crowned was crowned king of the Nemanjić dynasty's kingdom.
In one of his invocations to Zeus, Plethon presented him as the father of Poseidon and Kronos, which surprised many. Some scholars later concluded that Plethon must be assessed as a heretic.

Most modern historians agree that the ancient Greek religion had died out by the 9th century at the latest. In certain isolated areas, though, it survived until the 12th century, notably among the Tsakonia and the Maniots.

In medieval Bosnia, the Bosnian Church was a Christian church deemed heretical, yet some rulers were adherents of it. The Banate of Bosnia came into existence by 1154, amid Byzantine, Hungarian and Serbian influence.

In the mid-13th century, Pope Innocent IV criticized Italian merchants for exporting Bulgarian, Greek, and Ruthenian slaves to the Muslims in Jerusalem. It was a religious objection to a trade that ran along the Balkan religious border.

culture.text: Stećci are monumental medieval tombstones scattered across Bosnia and Herzegovina and nearby parts of Croatia, Montenegro and Serbia. About 60,000 stand in Bosnia and Herzegovina alone, and the custom peaked in the 14th and 15th centuries. It was shared by Bosnian, Catholic and Orthodox Church followers alike.

Monasteries were not built at Meteora in Thessaly until the 1300s, when monks looked for somewhere to hide from an increasing number of attacks by the Turks on Greece. Twenty-four monasteries were established atop the giant natural rock pillars, mainly from the second half of the 14th century under the rule of Simeon Uroš. Turkish raiders wanted the fertile plain of Thessaly and finally secured it in the second half of the 15th century. The complex is viewed locally as second in importance only to Mount Athos.

Hesychasm is a contemplative monastic tradition that seeks stillness through uninterrupted Jesus prayer. It took its definitive form in the 14th century at Mount Athos. The practitioners sometimes experienced God as light, called the uncreated light in the theology of St. Gregory Palamas.

Women are prohibited by Greek law and religious tradition from entering the area governed by the monastic community of Mount Athos. The peninsula is an important centre of Eastern Orthodox monasticism. Byzantine emperors granted its monastic settlements privileges and protection.

Athanasios the Meteorite brought followers from Mount Athos to Meteora in 1344 and founded the Great Meteoron monastery on the Broad Rock between 1356 and 1372. The site kept the monks safe from political upheaval. The only way up was a long ladder, which they drew up whenever they thought they were under threat. This gave them complete control of the entrance.

The Bogomils did not use the Christian cross or build churches, because they considered the body to be the temple. This gave rise to practices such as fasting or dancing to cleanse the body. The movement stayed strong and popular in the Balkans until the fall of the Second Bulgarian Empire at the end of the 14th century.

In Byzantine theology, a church building symbolized the Christian universe and reflected the splendor of heaven. A standardized program set the order of images: the most sacred figures went in the dome and apse, with scenes below arranged by religious importance. At Daphni, the Crucifixion scene shows Christ on the cross, with Mary and St. John at its foot, one on each side, against an empty golden background. Christ's body is drawn in a classic, athletic style, though its anatomy is not true to life.

In the Bosnian lands, the Bosnian Church was a Christian church deemed heretical, and some rulers adhered to it. Bosnian rulers empowered themselves through trade with Ragusa. Tvrtko I, who crowned himself king in 1377, brought Bosnia to its zenith.

The Ottoman capture of Thessaloniki in 1430 threw the Byzantine world into consternation. It was regarded, correctly, as a prelude to the fall of Constantinople itself. The memory of the event survived in folk traditions containing both fact and myths, including a Turkish tradition recorded by Apostolos Vacalopoulos.

The oldest known stećak with an inscription belongs to Marija, the wife of the priest Dabiživ. It carries a number and presumed year of 1231 and comes from Vidoštak near Stolac. Some stećci are richly decorated, and a few bear epitaphs.

St. Nicephorus the Hesychast, a 13th-century monk at Mount Athos, advised monks to bend their heads toward the chest and attach the prayer to their breathing. He also told them to fix their eyes during prayer on the middle of the body, concentrating the mind within the heart. This is the earliest attestation of such techniques in hesychast prayer, though Kallistos Ware says their origins may be far more ancient.

Gregory Sinaita learned a form of disciplined mental prayer from Arsenius of Crete. In 1310 he went to Mount Athos, where he remained until 1335 as a monk at the Skete of Magoula near Philotheou Monastery, introducing hesychast practice there.

After Frankish crusaders sacked Daphni Monastery in 1205, it passed to Cistercian monks from the Abbey of Bellevaux, who added a Gothic cloister. It became a popular burial place for Knights. The Cistercians abandoned it in 1458 after Sultan Mehmed II visited Athens.
The Greek prefix χατζι-, or xadzi-, comes from the Arabic hajji, meaning a Mecca pilgrim. In Medieval Greek it was used as a name affix for a Christian after a pilgrimage to Jerusalem.

Stećci took several forms. The chest (sanduk) and ridge-roofed (sljemenjak) types do not appear before the middle or end of the 14th century, while the upright pillar (stup) and cross (krstača) came no earlier than the mid-15th century. Upright forms may have been influenced by the nišan, the standing stone placed on Muslim graves.
